periods.activity_title: Entering the Poem: Sensory Memory and First Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond I (p.126): paired discussion on childhood memories, share with class.
Reflect and Respond II (p.126): discuss how mother–child relationships shape emotions and memory.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to recall a sound, scent, or sight that suddenly brought back a childhood moment. Two or three students share briefly; teacher connects these to how memory works through the senses, not through deliberate recollection.

Reflect and Respond I: students work in pairs to list two or three childhood memories they still carry clearly, then share their lists with the class. Teacher notes recurring themes on the board — songs, smells, places, faces.

Reflect and Respond II: class discusses together how a mother's presence — or absence — shapes what a child remembers and feels. Teacher draws out the idea that emotional bonds leave sensory imprints long after direct memory fades.

Teacher reads the poem aloud with deliberate pacing, students following in their textbooks (p.126). After the reading, teacher re-reads each stanza once more, pausing to let students mark the precise moment — tune, scent, sky — where the mother enters.

Teacher leads a whole-class conversation: which stanza felt closest to their own experience, and why? Students name the sense each stanza triggers. Teacher closes by naming Tagore as the poet and placing him briefly in the context of Bengali literary tradition.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading tasks work best when students feel safe sharing personal memories — keep the tone warm and unhurried before moving to the text. The poem's refrain ('I cannot remember my mother') is the emotional hinge of the whole work: ensure the read-aloud treats it as a recurring weight, not a neutral opener. Students who have not experienced bereavement may still connect through the poem's sensory approach; affirm that connection.

periods.activity_title: Stanza by Stanza: Comprehension and Poetic Devices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond III (p.126): match six key poem words to their meanings.
Check Your Understanding I (p.127–128): fill-in-the-blank comprehension for all three stanzas including setting.
Check Your Understanding II (p.128): complete the senses table — identify lines and sensory categories for each stanza.

time_bands.activity: Reflect and Respond III: students work individually to match the six words — hover, hum, cradle, shiuli, morning service, gaze — to their meanings (p.126), then pairs compare. Teacher corrects and asks students to use three of these words in one spoken sentence about the poem.

Check Your Understanding I: teacher guides the class stanza by stanza through the fill-in task (p.127–128). For each stanza students supply the missing information — the memory trigger, the setting, and the sensory detail — and teacher confirms answers through brief class discussion, ensuring everyone distinguishes indoor from outdoor settings correctly.

Check Your Understanding II: teacher displays the senses table structure on the board; students complete it for Stanzas 1, 2, and 3 (p.128), identifying the exact lines and the sense each line activates. Pairs compare, then the class builds a shared version on the board, with teacher drawing out why Tagore chose each sense for each stanza.

Teacher asks: if Tagore had written a fourth stanza, which sense has he not yet used — taste or touch — and what could the memory have been? A quick spoken round invites two or three creative responses before teacher closes the discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: The senses table is the conceptual scaffold for everything that follows in the poem's analysis — spend time ensuring students can explain WHY a line belongs to one sense category rather than simply labelling it. The shiuli flower (Stanza 2) is unfamiliar to many students; having its description ready from the poem's own lines (sweet fragrance, temple worship) will ground the olfactory discussion without needing outside information. Students who confuse 'auditory' and 'olfactory' benefit from saying the words aloud and connecting them to familiar Hindi/regional equivalents (shravan, gandh).

periods.activity_title: Devices, Tone, and Symbolism in Tagore's Lyric

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding III (p.128–129): eight-part analysis — alliteration, onomatopoeia, imagery, tone, title impact, refrain, symbolism.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the senses table completed earlier, naming the three stanzas' dominant images. Students then read the poem silently once more (p.126) before moving to the analytical questions, giving themselves a fresh encounter with the whole text.

Check Your Understanding III: teacher works through all eight sub-questions (p.128–129) as a structured class discussion. For alliteration and onomatopoeia, students locate and read examples aloud; for imagery, tone, and title-impact questions, the teacher elicits extended student responses and builds a class answer collaboratively on the board; for refrain and symbolism, students first write a sentence independently, then share and refine with the group.

Teacher draws together the devices covered — refrain, imagery, symbolism — and asks: how do these work together to create the poem's quietly melancholic tone? Three students give short responses. Teacher closes by naming the poem's structure (three parallel stanzas, each anchoring one sense) as itself a formal device — repetition of form mirrors repetition of loss.

periods.teacher_notes: The eight-part task is analytically rich; avoid racing through it — it is better to do the symbolism and tone questions thoroughly than to rush all eight. The question about the rhymeless poem's enjoyability often surprises students who associate 'good poetry' with rhyme; inviting them to listen to the poem's rhythm and the refrain's weight helps them hear free verse as a deliberate craft choice, not an absence. The self-study pointer: the critical reflection extracts (p.129–131) will be taken up in detail in a subsequent unit; students may read them independently ahead of that work.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for building class answers

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection: Close Reading of Two Extracts

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection I, Extract 1 (p.129–130): five-part close reading of the lullaby-tune stanza extract.
Critical Reflection I, Extract 2 (p.130–131): five-part close reading of the stillness-of-gaze sky extract.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the idea of close reading: the difference between understanding a poem and analysing how a specific set of lines achieves its effect. Students locate the first extract — the opening lines of Stanza 1 about the hovering tune — in their textbooks (p.129) and read it silently.

Critical Reflection I, Extract 1: teacher leads students through all five sub-questions (p.129–130) — the emotion conveyed by the hovering tune, the role of the tune during playtime, whether the experience is occasional or constant, and how the mother's presence is felt without physical proximity. Students write brief answers individually first, then discuss each with the class; teacher presses for textual evidence with each response.

Critical Reflection I, Extract 2: students locate the Stanza 3 lines about the stillness of the mother's gaze spreading over the sky (p.130). Teacher leads the five sub-questions (p.130–131) — what the sky symbolises, what emotion 'stillness' carries, whether the gaze is literal or figurative, the purpose of the comparison, and the tone of the extract. Paired discussion precedes each class-level answer.

Teacher asks: both extracts use something non-physical — a tune, a gaze — to represent the mother. What does this tell us about what the poem is really about? One or two spoken responses close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The two extracts together show the poem's movement from sound (Stanza 1) to sight (Stanza 3), skipping directly over the olfactory middle stanza — worth noting to students as evidence that the extracts are a selection, not the whole poem. Students sometimes read the sky image literally (the mother is watching from the sky as a spirit); the close-reading questions should gently redirect them toward the symbolism the poem actually employs — the sky as an extension of a remembered gaze. The symbolism analysis completed earlier (Check Your Understanding III) is the content foundation this unit builds on.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection II (p.131): four extended-answer questions on refrain impact, nature's role, and mother–child perception.
Vocabulary in Context I (p.131): classify twenty-five sensory words into Visual, Auditory, Olfactory, Tactile categories.

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context II (p.132): fill seven blanks in the Sarojini Naidu March morning passage with appropriate sensory words.

time_bands.activity: Critical Reflection II: teacher poses each of the four questions (p.131) in turn — the emotional impact of the refrain, the symbolic connection between the mother and shiuli flowers and the humming tune, nature's role as a carrier of memory, and what the poem infers about the mother–child bond. Students write a sentence or two in response to each, then contribute to an open class discussion that the teacher shapes into a coherent interpretive account of the poem.

Vocabulary in Context I: teacher introduces the twenty-five sensory words (p.131) and explains the four categories. Students classify all words individually, then pairs compare and resolve disagreements. Teacher confirms answers and asks students to read three of their choices aloud in a sentence that connects the word to the poem's imagery — for example, using 'fragrant' in a sentence about the shiuli.

Teacher bridges the two activities: Tagore builds the poem almost entirely from sensory vocabulary — the very words students just classified are the building blocks of poetic imagery. Teacher sets the Sarojini Naidu fill-in task (p.132) as home reading and individual written work.

periods.teacher_notes: The Critical Reflection II questions are the highest-demand analytical moment in this poem's reading spine; allow students time to write before speaking, as the questions on nature's role and the mother–child inference reward careful thought. The sensory vocabulary task anchors the abstract literary concept of imagery in concrete word-level recognition — the two activities reinforce each other when sequenced as above. Vocabulary in Context III (p.132, the picture-matching task) is not anchored in this plan; it can be used as a self-study extension by interested students.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond I (p.133): match six statements to four speakers sharing childhood memories; two statements unused.
Speaking Activity I (p.133): paired oral presentation — an object, song, or place that carries a personal memory, using sensory detail and structured prompts.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the listening task: students will hear four brief accounts of childhood memories and must match six statements to the correct speaker, with two statements unused. Teacher distributes or directs students to the statement list (p.133) and allows a moment to read through all six before the transcript is read.

Listen and Respond I: teacher reads the transcript of all four speakers aloud at a measured pace (transcript, p.266). Students note their matches as they listen. Teacher reads the transcript a second time; students finalise their answers. Class shares responses and teacher confirms the correct matches, briefly explaining why the two unused statements do not fit any speaker.

Teacher introduces the speaking task: each student thinks of one object, song, or place that carries a significant personal memory (p.133). Teacher displays the five structured prompts on the board — introduce, describe with sensory detail, narrate the specific memory, explain impact, summarise why it matters. Students take two minutes to make brief notes.

Speaking Activity I: pairs take turns presenting their memory to each other using the five-prompt structure. Teacher circulates, listening for sensory language and prompting any student who stays only at the level of plot ('we went to the beach') to add a sensory or emotional detail. Three or four volunteers then share with the whole class.

Teacher closes by asking the class: Tagore's poem and the four speakers all recover memories through sensation — what does that tell us about how memory works? One or two spoken responses close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task's two unused statements (about parents urging adventure and about school days as a source of keeping in touch) require students to read carefully — they are plausible distractors. Reading the transcript twice at an even pace, rather than rushing, is essential for fair listening conditions. In the speaking task, encourage students to move beyond narrative into sensory and emotional detail; the sentence starters on p.133 are scaffolds, not scripts — students who rely on them too heavily should be gently asked to personalise their language.
materials: Transcript text for teacher (p.266 of the textbook)

periods.activity_title: From Poem to Page: Writing, Memory, and the World Beyond Tagore

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task I (p.133): diary entry describing a sensory-rich school trip — format, first person, sensory detail, emotion, reflection.
Learning Beyond the Text II (p.135): share and discuss poems and songs on family and memory from English and own language; read Thomas Hood's 'I Remember, I Remember'.

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text I (p.134): research unique flowers of India — appearance, scent, location, historical significance — and add to the shiuli list.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the synthesis by naming what the chapter has explored together: how Tagore uses the senses — sound, scent, sight — to recover a presence that direct memory cannot reach, and how the same impulse appeared in the listening extracts and speaking activity. Teacher asks: what form would you choose to write down a sensory memory — a poem, a story, a letter, a diary entry? Students respond briefly.

Writing Task I: teacher introduces the diary entry task (p.133) — imagining a school trip that engaged all the senses. Teacher models the diary format on the board (day, date, time; first-person voice; opening sensory detail; emotional moment; closing reflection). Students plan in two minutes, then draft their complete diary entries individually. With about five minutes remaining in this band, pairs exchange entries and offer one observation on the strongest sensory image their partner used.

Learning Beyond the Text II: teacher asks two or three students to share a poem or song about family or childhood memory — in any language they know. Teacher then reads Thomas Hood's 'I Remember, I Remember' aloud (p.135). Students note one image from Hood that resembles Tagore's approach and one that differs. A brief class comparison follows: both poets remember a childhood place through images — what does each poem suggest about the emotional texture of that remembering?

Teacher closes the chapter by returning to Tagore's refrain: 'I cannot remember my mother' — and asks whether, having worked through the poem, the class now reads that line as a statement of loss or of presence. Students vote by show of hands and one student from each side gives a reason. Teacher sets the flowers research task (p.134) as independent follow-up work.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit brings together the poem's sensory logic, the functional writing skill of diary form, and the comparative literary encounter with Thomas Hood — all without requiring any specific earlier activity to have occurred. If some students have already engaged with the shiuli research informally, their knowledge can enrich the Thomas Hood comparison, but the unit runs fully without it. The diary entry is designed to be completed within this sitting — planning, drafting, and peer response all happen here, so no writing is carried forward unfinished.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for diary format model

items.source_context: Tagore's three-stanza lyric recovering a lost mother through auditory, olfactory, and visual sense-memory.
items.item_stem: In Tagore's poem, each of the three stanzas is anchored to a different human sense. Which of the following correctly pairs the stanza with its dominant sense?

options.label: A
options.text: Stanza 1 — auditory; Stanza 2 — olfactory; Stanza 3 — visual

options.label: B
options.text: Stanza 1 — auditory; Stanza 2 — visual; Stanza 3 — olfactory

options.label: C
options.text: Stanza 1 — olfactory; Stanza 2 — visual; Stanza 3 — auditory

options.label: D
options.text: Stanza 1 — visual; Stanza 2 — auditory; Stanza 3 — olfactory

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses the senses: misassigns olfactory to Stanza 1 (the lullaby stanza) and overlooks the shiuli scent in Stanza 2.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses auditory and visual and misplaces the olfactory, suggesting the student has not mapped the stanzas systematically.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Correctly places auditory in Stanza 1 but swaps olfactory and visual between Stanzas 2 and 3.

items.source_lo: Student analyses sensory imagery, poetic devices, symbolism, and the emotional architecture of a lyric poem using poetry as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Tagore's three-stanza lyric recovering a lost mother through auditory, olfactory, and visual sense-memory.
items.item_stem:
Read the second stanza on p.127, beginning “I cannot remember my mother / but when in the early autumn morning”.

1. Tagore chooses the shiuli flower and the scent of the morning temple service to represent the mother in this stanza. What does the pairing of these two images — a flower and a religious ritual — suggest about the speaker's unconscious perception of his mother's character?
2. The third stanza shifts from scent to sight: the stillness of the mother's gaze 'has spread all over the sky.' Analyse how the shift from an enclosed, olfactory image (a flower in the air) to an expansive, visual image (the sky) reflects the poem's emotional movement from intimate memory to a sense of eternal presence.
3. Tagore opens all three stanzas with the same line: 'I cannot remember my mother.' Evaluate whether this refrain functions as an admission of loss or as a rhetorical device that paradoxically asserts the mother's presence. Use evidence from at least two stanzas in your answer.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the second stanza on p.127, beginning “I cannot remember my mother / but when in the early autumn morning”.

expected_elements: Q1: Notes the mother as gentle, devotional, and pure — mirrored in the flower and worship.
Q1: Connects both images to spiritual or ritualistic associations beyond the purely domestic.
Q2: Identifies the movement from a localised, passing scent to an infinite, permanent visual field.
Q2: Links the sky's vastness to the idea that the mother's presence is not bounded by time or place.
Q3: Argues the refrain is paradoxical — denying memory while enacting it through sensory recall in each stanza.

items.source_lo: Student listens to spoken accounts of personal memory, identifies key information, and matches it to descriptive statements using focused listening strategies.
items.source_context: Four speakers describe childhood memories — a grandfather's encouragement, carefree outdoor play, grandparents' comic-strip stories, and a changed seaside home.
items.item_stem:
You will hear four short accounts of childhood memories. Read the statements below before listening. After listening, decide whether each statement is True or False. Write T or F, and for each FALSE statement write one word or phrase from the account that shows it is incorrect.
(1) Speaker (i)'s grandfather encouraged the speaker by asking competitive questions about bravery.
(2) Speaker (ii) describes indoor hobbies like reading and drawing as the heart of childhood freedom.
(3) Speaker (iii) pretended to retell his grandfather's comic-strip stories but ended up muddling the details.
(4) Speaker (iv) found the seaside unchanged and as peaceful as remembered after returning a decade later.

options.text: Speaker (i)'s grandfather encouraged the speaker by asking competitive questions about bravery.
Speaker (ii) describes indoor hobbies like reading and drawing as the heart of childhood freedom.
Speaker (iii) pretended to retell his grandfather's comic-strip stories but ended up muddling the details.
Speaker (iv) found the seaside unchanged and as peaceful as remembered after returning a decade later.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True: the grandfather asked 'who is the bravest one?' and the speaker shouted 'Me', showing competitive encouragement. 2 — False: Speaker (ii) describes outdoor activities — chasing butterflies, making paper boats, playing on sandy beaches — not indoor hobbies. 3 — True: Speaker (iii) says they ended up babbling and forgetting the real narratives when retelling in the kitchen. 4 — False: the beach was 'now crowded' and the carefree days were 'replaced by a sense of distance'; it was not the same.

items.source_lo: Student listens to spoken accounts of personal memory, identifies key information, and matches it to descriptive statements using focused listening strategies.
items.source_context: Four speakers describe childhood memories — a grandfather's encouragement, carefree outdoor play, grandparents' comic-strip stories, and a changed seaside home.
items.item_stem: Among the four speakers, two describe memories in which a grandparent plays a central role, and two describe memories centred on a place or activity. In 2–3 sentences, explain what the grandparent-centred memories (Speakers i and iii) share in common, and how Speaker (iv)'s account differs from all three in its emotional outcome.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Speakers (i) and (iii) both find that a grandparent's words or stories remain vivid and uplifting long after the experience — one through the grandfather's rallying question about bravery, the other through the cheerful chaos of retelling comic-strip tales. Speaker (iv) differs because the memory concludes with a sense of loss and distance: returning to the seaside reveals that both the place and the family closeness have changed, leaving the speaker with a melancholic rather than a sustaining recollection.

items.item_stem: Think of a sound — a piece of music, a voice, or an everyday noise — that instantly brings back a specific memory. In a short talk to a partner, introduce the sound, describe what it sounds like in detail, narrate the memory it unlocks, explain why it affects you even now, and close with a reflection on what this tells you about how memory works.

expected_elements: Introduces the sound clearly with a specific name or description.
Uses at least one sensory detail beyond sound — a connected smell, image, or feeling.
Narrates a concrete, specific memory linked to the sound.
Reflects on why the sound retains emotional power in the present.
Closes with a generalisation or insight about sensory memory.

items.item_stem: Tagore's poem suggests that a person can be powerfully present in memory even when they cannot be directly recalled. Do you agree that sensory triggers — a smell, a sound, a sight — are more reliable carriers of memory than deliberate recollection? Argue your position with at least two reasons, and be prepared to respond to a classmate who holds the opposite view.

expected_elements: States a clear position — agree or disagree — at the outset.
Gives two distinct reasons supported by personal or observed examples.
References the poem's use of the lullaby tune, shiuli scent, or sky image as evidence.
Acknowledges and responds to a counterargument with a reasoned rebuttal.
Maintains a formal enough register appropriate for a class debate context.

items.item_stem: Write a diary entry in which you describe your first visit to a busy city heritage monument — a fort, a step-well, or an old mosque or temple. Begin with the day, date, and time of the visit. Use first-person voice throughout. Capture at least two distinct sensory details (what you saw, heard, or smelled), describe one moment that felt particularly striking, and close with a brief personal reflection on what the visit made you think or feel.

expected_elements: Opens with correct diary format: day, date, time, and a salutation or direct opening.
Maintains first-person voice consistently throughout the entry.
Includes at least two specific sensory details — visual, auditory, or olfactory.
Describes one striking moment with enough specificity to feel real.
Closes with a reflective sentence that moves beyond description to personal meaning.

items.item_stem: A local cultural magazine is running a series called 'Places That Speak'. Write a short piece (200–250 words) for the magazine in which you argue that one particular public place in your town or city — a market, a railway station, a riverbank — deserves to be remembered and preserved because of the sensory and emotional experience it offers visitors. Use specific sensory language, give at least one concrete reason for preservation, and address your piece to general readers who may never have visited this place.

expected_elements: Identifies a specific, named public place and addresses general readers clearly.
Uses vivid sensory language — at least two distinct senses — to evoke the place.
Advances at least one clear, reasoned argument for why the place deserves preservation.
Adopts a persuasive register appropriate for a magazine piece — engaging and somewhat formal.
Closes with a call to action or a memorable image that reinforces the argument.

Column A|Column B
pungent|(i) Auditory
squeaky|(ii) Visual
crimson|(iii) Tactile
slimy|(iv) Olfactory
deafening|(v) Auditory

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: pungent — (iv) Olfactory; squeaky — (i) Auditory; crimson — (ii) Visual; slimy — (iii) Tactile; deafening — (v) Auditory

items.source_context: Classifying twenty-five sensory words and completing a sensory-language passage in the spirit of Tagore's imagery.
items.item_stem:
The passage below describes an early morning in Tagore's garden, but six sensory words have been removed. Choose the most appropriate word from the box to fill each blank. Write the word against each blank number. Not all words in the box will be used.

Box: fragrant · deafening · gloomy · vibrant · stale · shrill · chilled · glowing

The garden woke slowly. A (1) ___ breeze, carrying the scent of night-blooming flowers, moved between the trees. The light was (2) ___, soft and golden at the edges, as the sun climbed above the wall. From somewhere close, a (3) ___ call of a koel broke the quiet. The damp grass felt (4) ___ under bare feet. Near the temple gate, the air turned (5) ___ with incense and marigold. A pair of bulbuls made the branches (6) ___ with colour as they darted from flower to flower.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — fragrant; 2 — glowing; 3 — shrill; 4 — chilled; 5 — fragrant (accept: vibrant for sense of richness, but fragrant is the stronger contextual fit near incense); 6 — vibrant. Accept near-synonyms where the sensory category and contextual register are correct.

items.source_lo: Student explores multilingual and cross-cultural literary treatments of childhood memory and familial longing, comparing themes and imagery across poems from different traditions.
items.source_context: Thomas Hood's 'I Remember, I Remember' set alongside student-shared poems and songs on family memory from their own languages.
items.item_stem: Tagore's poem and Thomas Hood's 'I Remember, I Remember' both use specific images from a remembered childhood to convey emotional longing. In a well-developed paragraph, compare how each poet uses one image from nature or the domestic world to express the feeling of loss or distance from the past. State clearly what image each poet uses, what feeling it conveys, and what the comparison reveals about the two poets' different approaches to remembering.

expected_elements: Names one specific image from each poem — e.g. Tagore's shiuli scent or sky-gaze; Hood's roses, laburnum, or the window through which the sun came peeping.
Explains what emotional state or sense of loss each image carries for its speaker.
Draws a clear comparison: similarity or difference in how each image functions — e.g. both use natural images, but Tagore's evoke an absent person while Hood's mark an absent time.
Shows awareness that Tagore's poem moves inward (sensation unlocking presence) while Hood's moves outward (a list of external remembered scenes).
Writes in a formal, analytical register appropriate for a comparative literary paragraph.

items.source_lo: Student explores multilingual and cross-cultural literary treatments of childhood memory and familial longing, comparing themes and imagery across poems from different traditions.
items.source_context: Thomas Hood's 'I Remember, I Remember' set alongside student-shared poems and songs on family memory from their own languages.
items.item_stem: Design a short interdisciplinary project (described in 150–200 words) that explores the theme of sensory memory across two languages or cultural traditions — one being the language of Tagore's poem (English translation of Bengali) and one being a language you know. Your project description should: name the second language or tradition; identify at least one poem, song, or story from that tradition that deals with childhood or familial memory; explain what sensory images it uses; and propose one way your class could present the comparison (e.g. a bilingual poster, a recorded reading, a short written essay).

expected_elements: Names a specific second language or cultural tradition with a clear rationale.
Identifies a real or plausibly described poem, song, or story from that tradition.
Describes at least one sensory image from the chosen work and connects it to the theme of memory.
Proposes a concrete, feasible presentation format for the comparison.
Demonstrates awareness that the same theme of longing or childhood memory appears across cultures and languages.
